t: Are You Afraid To Hold Students Accountable? https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2014/12/13/are-you-afraid-to-hold-students-accountable/
q: Many teachers become so committed to this one important strategy that they lose perspective. They go too far. They venture beyond effective means of building rapport and into unhealthy deference.

They fear that if they truly hold them accountable, the relationship will suffer. Their students won’t like them anymore, and they’ll lose the precious influence they’ve worked so hard to achieve. But it isn’t true.
In fact, when you let misbehavior go without a consequence, when you let poorly followed routines slide and difficult students off the hook, you lose influence. You never gain it.
If you fear accountability, your students will walk all over you. They’ll become flippant and blasé, brazen and disrespectful.
One of the most overlooked aspects of building a strong relationship with students is your ability to protect them from disruption, disorder, chaos, and the like.
In the hands of a fair and consistent teacher, accountability works. It works in the suburbs and in the inner city. It works in the backwoods, the small town, and the largest metropolis.
x: Building rapport is essential to classroom management, but some teachers overcorrect into unhealthy deference, avoiding accountability out of fear of damaging the relationship.

t: When (And Why) You Should Ignore Crying Students udents/
q: But doing so in the moments after enforcing a consequence is a mistake.
Some students have learned from experience that if they cry, they have a good chance of avoiding consequence.

In any case, reflecting on their misbehavior, as well as on those who may have been affected by it, is a good thing. And the worst thing we can do is interrupt this process, sugarcoat their actions, or let them off the hook.
If every time a student cries you immediately rush to their side, then you’re going to find yourself doing it a lot.
If you make it a point to ignore crying, dramatics, and the like in the aftermath of misbehavior, then your students will stop doing it.
It’s a good idea to let them know that there are no hard feelings, that you never hold a grudge, and that forgiveness is always and forever extended.
x: Michael Linsin addresses the instinct to comfort a crying student immediately after enforcing a consequence, arguing this well-meaning response is usually a mistake.
